label: Shemu'el Bet (2 Samuel) — Part 4 — Chapters 19–24
summary_plain: Dawid returns to Yerushalayim after Avshalom's death. Sheva ben Bikhri leads a rebellion — every man to his tents, O Yisra'EL! Yo'av crushes the revolt. The Giv'onites demand justice for Sha'ul's violation of the covenant with them — Dawid delivers seven of Sha'ul's descendants. Ritzpah guards their bodies on the rock. YHWH sends a three-year famine because Sha'ul broke the covenant with the Giv'onites. Dawid's mighty warriors are listed — the thirty and the three. Dawid's census angers YHWH — a pestilence strikes Yisra'EL. Dawid purchases the threshing floor of Aravnah the Yevusite and builds an altar. YHWH relents from the plague. Dawid's song of praise: YHWH is my rock, my fortress, my deliverer.
summary_scholarly: The ACR reads from 4QSam-a and the Orit Ge'ez. Dawid's song (ch 22) parallels Tehillim 18 — the DSS Psalms scroll (11QPsa) preserves independent witness to the psalm tradition. The Giv'onite episode (ch 21) demonstrates YHWH's commitment to covenant justice across generations — a covenant made with non-Israelites (Yehoshua 9) is enforced by YHWH against Yisra'EL's own king. The census (ch 24) establishes the site of the future Temple — the threshing floor of Aravnah the Yevusite. 4QSam-a preserves variant readings in the warrior lists (ch 23) that differ from the Masoretic and the parallel account in 1 Divre ha-Yamim 11.

key_terms.definition: After Avshalom's death, David's return to Yerushalayim is politically complex (2 Shemu'el 19). The northern tribes are angry that Yehudah acted first to bring David back. Shimei begs forgiveness and is pardoned. Mefivoshet meets David looking unkempt. Barzillai the Gileadite is honored. The rift between Yehudah and the northern tribes foreshadows the eventual kingdom split.

A Binyaminite man who sounds a trumpet and calls: 'We have no share in David, no part in the son of Yishai — every man to his tent, Yisra'el!' (2 Shemu'el 20:1). He leads a brief northern rebellion after Avshalom's defeat. Yoav pursues him to the city of Avel Bet-Ma'akhah. The city's wise woman negotiates — she drops Sheva's head over the wall to Yoav, ending the rebellion.

The unnamed wise woman of Avel Bet-Ma'akhah who intervenes when Yoav besieges her city to capture Sheva ben Bikhri. She calls to Yoav and negotiates: Avel is 'a mother in Yisra'el,' a city of peaceable and faithful people. Why would Yoav destroy it? Yoav says he only wants Sheva. She promises to drop his head over the wall — and does. One woman ends the rebellion and saves her city.

Sha'ul's concubine who spreads sackcloth on a rock and guards the bodies of Sha'ul's seven descendants from exposure to birds and wild animals (2 Shemu'el 21:8-10). She watches from the beginning of harvest until the rains come. When David hears of her vigil, he collects the bones of Sha'ul and Yehonatan from Yavesh-Gilad and buries them all honorably in the tomb of Qish. Rizpah's covenant faithfulness prompts David's covenant action.

A three-year famine in David's reign is attributed to Sha'ul's earlier slaughter of the Gibeonites — a people Yehoshua had made a covenant with. YHWH reveals this to David (2 Shemu'el 21). David goes to the Gibeonites and asks what atonement they require. They ask for seven of Sha'ul's descendants to be handed over. David hands them seven sons/grandsons of Sha'ul, excluding Mefivoshet for the sake of his covenant with Yehonatan. The famine ends.

In 2 Shemu'el 24, David orders a census of all fighting men in Yisra'el and Yehudah — Yoav tries to dissuade him. After nine months the count is 800,000 in Yisra'el and 500,000 in Yehudah. David immediately recognizes he has sinned. YHWH offers three punishments through the prophet Gad: three years of famine, three months of fleeing enemies, or three days of plague. David chooses the plague — preferring to fall into YHWH's hands rather than human hands.

David's prophet (also mentioned in 1 Shemu'el) who brings YHWH's three-option punishment after the census. Gad also commands David to build an altar at Aravnah's threshing floor. David obeys, purchases the threshing floor from Aravnah, and builds the altar. YHWH answers his prayer and the plague stops. This site — the threshing floor of Aravnah the Yevusite — becomes the location of Shlomoh's Temple.

The site on Mount Moriyah where David builds an altar after the plague (2 Shemu'el 24:18-25). Aravnah (also called Ornan in Chronicles) offers to give David the threshing floor, the oxen, and everything for free. David refuses: 'I will not sacrifice to YHWH my Creator burnt offerings that cost me nothing.' He pays 50 shekels of silver and builds the altar. This site becomes the future location of Shlomoh's Temple.

In 2 Shemu'el 22 (essentially the same as Psalm 18), David sings a great poem thanking YHWH for deliverance from all his enemies and from Sha'ul. YHWH is his rock, his fortress, his deliverer, his shield. He describes YHWH's coming in storm imagery — smoke from His nostrils, fire from His mouth, He rode on a cherub and flew on the wings of the wind. The song spans all of David's life and stands as his theological testimony.

In 2 Shemu'el 23:1-7, David speaks his 'last words' — a brief oracle in which he describes himself as 'the man exalted by the Most High, the anointed of the Creator of Ya'akov, Yisra'el's singer of songs.' He describes the ideal king who rules in the fear of YHWH — like the light of morning, like the sun rising. Then he acknowledges his own house is not like that before YHWH, but YHWH has made an everlasting covenant with him. The 'last words' appear before the account of David's mighty warriors.

faq.question: Why is the census a sin?
faq.answer: The text does not explain the reason directly — it simply records that David's heart struck him after taking the census and he confessed 'I have sinned greatly.' Several explanations exist in the tradition: a census may have implied David was counting on military manpower rather than on YHWH; a census in ancient practice required payment of a half-shekel ransom to avoid plague (Shemot 30:12) and this may not have been done; or the census represented a royal assertion of control over the people that transgressed covenant boundaries. What the text emphasizes is David's immediate recognition and confession, and YHWH's graded response that still allows David to choose.

faq.question: What is the significance of the threshing floor of Aravnah as the Temple site?
faq.answer: The threshing floor of Aravnah becomes the location of Shlomoh's Temple (confirmed in 2 Divrei HaYamim/Chronicles 3:1, which identifies it as Mount Moriyah). By purchasing the site himself with silver — refusing the gift — David ensures that the Temple's future location is bought, not donated. David's altar and the stopping of the plague at that exact spot mark it as the place where YHWH's anger was appeased. The site carries enormous theological weight: it is purchased, it is the place where plague stopped, and it is on the mountain later identified with the covenant sacrifice of Bereshit 22.

faq.question: Who was Rizpah and what does her vigil accomplish?
faq.answer: Rizpah bat Ayah was Sha'ul's concubine — the same woman Avner was accused of sleeping with, which triggered the break between Avner and Ish-Boshet. When seven of Sha'ul's descendants are executed to satisfy the Gibeonites, she spreads sackcloth on a rock and stands guard over their exposed bodies from the beginning of harvest through the rains — refusing to let birds or wild animals touch them. Proper burial was essential to honor in ancient Hebrew culture; exposure was a mark of disgrace and divine curse. Her determined, months-long vigil draws David's attention and leads him to retrieve and bury Sha'ul and Yehonatan's bones from Yavesh-Gilad.

faq.question: What does the Gibeonite episode reveal about covenant obligations?
faq.answer: The Gibeonites had a covenant with Yisra'el dating back to Yehoshua — they had deceived Yehoshua into making peace with them, but the covenant was ratified by oath (invoking YHWH) and therefore binding. Sha'ul's later slaughter of Gibeonites violated this ancient covenant oath. The famine that results is YHWH's judgment not primarily for the killing but for the broken covenant. When David asks the Gibeonites what atonement they need, he is treating their covenant claim as legally valid — even a covenant made under false pretenses is binding once sworn before YHWH.

faq.question: What is the significance of the tension between Yehudah and the northern tribes at David's return?
faq.answer: In 2 Shemu'el 19, Yehudah acts first to bring David back across the Yarden, and the northern tribes — who had a larger portion of the military — feel excluded and dishonored. The argument becomes heated: 'We have ten shares in the king — we are the ones who first spoke of bringing back the king.' But Yehudah prevailed. This resentment does not disappear; it re-ignites immediately in Sheva ben Bikhri's rebellion. And decades later, after Shlomoh's death, the same wound opens permanently: 'We have no share in David.' The kingdom splits along exactly this fault line.

faq.question: What does David's choice of plague reveal about his theology?
faq.answer: When YHWH offers three punishments — famine (human suffering over time), fleeing enemies (falling into human hands), or plague (direct divine judgment over three days) — David chooses the plague. His reasoning: 'Let us fall into the hands of YHWH, for his mercy is great; but do not let me fall into human hands.' David trusts YHWH's character more than any human power's restraint. He has experienced YHWH's mercy and forgiveness personally (the Bat-Sheva confession). He prefers a known, merciful YHWH over unpredictable human cruelty. The plague kills 70,000 people, but it also stops when YHWH relents — exactly as David predicted.

faq.question: Who are the 'mighty warriors' listed in 2 Shemu'el 23?
faq.answer: The list in 2 Shemu'el 23:8-39 names David's elite soldiers, beginning with the Three (the most elite) and the Thirty (a wider circle of champions). The Three are Yashov'am (or Yoshev-Bashebet), El'azar ben Dodo, and Shammah ben Agee. Notable deeds include: defending a plot of lentils alone against the Plishtim; going into the Plishtim camp to draw water from a well in Bet-Lekhem at David's offhand wish (David pours it out as a libation to YHWH, refusing to drink what cost blood). Uriyah the Hittite appears at the end of the list — a final indictment of David's betrayal of one of his own heroes.

faq.question: What is the structure of the end of Shemu'el Bet and why does it end this way?
faq.answer: The final chapters of 2 Shemu'el (21-24) form a symmetrical appendix structured around Avshalom's rebellion narrative. Two episodes of national crisis (Gibeonite atonement and census/plague) frame two lists of David's warriors and two poems (David's song and last words). This creates an artistic chiasm rather than pure chronological narrative. The book ends with David purchasing the Temple site — positioning Shlomoh's future work as the fulfillment of David's whole story. The placement of Uriyah at the end of the warrior list, after the census episode, is likely a deliberate editorial choice that keeps the moral reckoning of David's greatest sin visible to the end.

faq.question: What does Sheva ben Bikhri's rebellion reveal about David's kingdom?
faq.answer: Sheva's rebellion, coming immediately on the heels of Avshalom's, shows how fragile the unified kingdom actually is. All it takes is one Binyaminite sounding a horn and invoking tribal identity — 'we have no share in David' — for the northern tribes to follow a nobody. David's response is swift and effective: Yoav pursues Sheva relentlessly. But the fact that Sheva's call finds immediate followers reveals that Avshalom's rebellion did not resolve the underlying political tension — it only deferred it. The kingdom is held together by David's personal authority, not by institutional unity, and the moment that personal authority is questioned, the structure strains.

faq.question: What does David's great song in chapter 22 tell us about his faith?
faq.answer: David's song in 2 Shemu'el 22 (preserved also as Psalm 18) is a comprehensive theological statement. YHWH is his rock, fortress, deliverer, shield, stronghold. When he cried in distress, YHWH heard from His Temple — the entire cosmos shook. YHWH came in storm, thundered from heaven, shot lightning as arrows. He rescued David because YHWH delighted in him. The theology is direct and personal: YHWH acts for David specifically, not abstractly. The song also claims David's own righteousness as the basis for YHWH's favor — not because David is sinless, but because he maintained covenant loyalty and did not turn from YHWH's decrees. It is covenant theology in poetic form.
